newsitem.title: USA: After McVeigh's arrest, an explosive note found.
newsitem.headline: After McVeigh's arrest, an explosive note found.

text.p: The state trooper who arrested Oklahoma City bombing defendant Timothy McVeigh said on Monday he found a handwritten note about the need to buy more explosives in a patrol car where McVeigh had sat.
"TNT, $5 a stick. Need more. Call after 1 May, see if I can get some more," read the notation on the back of a business card, Oklahoma State Trooper Charles Hanger said.

Hanger arrested McVeigh north of Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995, after noticing his yellow 1977 Mercury Marquis had no license plate. It was the same day as the bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that killed 168 people.
Several days later, Hanger said, he found the card with the note and submitted it as evidence. "I took the card to the command post in Oklahoma City and asked it be turned over to the FBI," he said.

Hanger was the 10th witness to take the stand in the Oklahoma City bombing trial. The first nine were survivors, rescuers and victims' relatives who described in chilling detail the devastation of the bombing.
McVeigh, who has pleaded not guilty to the bombing and faces the death penalty if convicted, watched the proceedings intently but showed no emotion.

Hanger testified that when he arrested McVeigh the Gulf War veteran was armed with a semi-automatic pistol. "I noticed he had a bulge under his left arm," he said. He asked McVeigh to open his jacket slowly and McVeigh told him, "I have a weapon."

Hanger, who testified he had no idea that McVeigh might be linked to the bombing when he arrested him, asked McVeigh why he carried the pistol. "He felt he had the right to carry it for his protection," he said McVeigh told him.

The semi-automatic pistol contained a black talon bullet, the type that expands after entering a body, causing greater injury than a standard bullet. McVeigh also told the trooper that he had a knife.
Under cross-examination by defence counsel, Hanger said McVeigh was cooperative during the arrest.

The prosecution also tried to establish the integrity of the evidence collected from McVeigh by showing it was not contaminated. Hanger testified that his patrol car was new when he received it and that it had not been used to transport explosives or transport individuals who had been charged with possession of explosives.

The defence has claimed the evidence was not sufficiently secure at the jail but Hanger told the court he did not know of any cases where a prisoner's belongings were disturbed at the Noble County jail. He said the evidence collected from McVeigh was locked up and secure from potential tampering.
